title: LINEAR ALGEBRA
body:
Linear algebra is the study of [[System of Linear Equations|linear systems]] and the objects
that solve them: [[Vector|vectors]], [[Matrix|matrices]], and the
[[Linear Transformation|transformations]] matrices represent. The restriction to *linear* looks
severe (no squares, no products of variables, no trig) and it buys something enormous: linear
problems can be solved mechanically, in polynomial time, in any number of dimensions. Almost
everything that is computationally tractable is either linear or is being approximated by
something linear.

For this degree it is the most reused mathematics in the building. A [[Forward Pass]] through a
neural network *is* [[Matrix Multiplication]]; a neuron's weighted sum *is* a [[Dot Product]];
PCA and dimensionality reduction *are* [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] of a covariance matrix.
[[MACHINE LEARNING]] is downstream of this note by a shorter path than of any other MATH course.
It also supplies structure the later MATH courses generalise: [[Vector Space]] is an algebraic
structure in the same sense a [[Group]] is, and the [[Complex Numbers]] chapter is where
[[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] starts.

The single organising idea, if you keep one: **choosing the right [[Basis]] is how you turn a
hard problem into an easy one.** [[Diagonalization]] is that idea with the details filled in.

## Topics

### Systems and how to solve them

- [[System of Linear Equations]]: what a linear system is, and why the solution set is always
  none, one, or infinitely many, never exactly two
- [[Gaussian Elimination]]: the algorithm. Augmented matrices, the three row operations, echelon
  and reduced echelon form, elementary matrices, and the $O(n^3)$ cost
- [[Matrix Inverse]]: what plays the role of division, when it exists, and the equivalence table
  that most of the first half of the course quietly runs on
- [[Cramer's Rule]]: a closed form for the solution, and a demonstration that a closed form is
  not the same as a good algorithm

### Matrices

- [[Matrix]]: notation, addition, scalar multiplication, transpose, and the special shapes
  (identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric)
- [[Matrix Multiplication]]: the row-by-column rule, and why it is composition of functions
  rather than an arbitrary convention
- [[Non-Commutative]]: $AB \neq BA$, in three separate ways

### Determinants

- [[Determinant]]: one number saying how much a matrix scales volume, and whether it flips
  orientation. Zero means collapsed, which means not invertible
- Cofactor expansion, evaluation by row reduction, and the multiplicative property
  $\det(AB) = \det A \det B$, all in the same note
- [[Cramer's Rule]] again, as the application

### Vectors and vector spaces

- [[Vector]]: an ordered list of $n$ numbers, the arrow picture and where it stops working, norm
  and distance
- [[Dot Product]]: multiplying two vectors into a number, and where angle, orthogonality, and
  projection come from
- [[Vector Space]]: the ten axioms, subspaces, linear combinations and span, and the point that
  matrices, polynomials, functions, and ODE solutions are all vector spaces
- [[Linear Dependence]]: testing a set for redundancy
- [[Basis]]: independent **and** spanning, the coordinates it gives you, dimension, and
  orthonormal bases

### Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

- [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]: the directions a matrix does not turn. The characteristic
  equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$, eigenspaces, and what an eigenvector actually means
- [[Diagonalization]]: $A = PDP^{-1}$, when it is possible, and why matrix powers and systems of
  [[Differential Equations]] both fall out of it

### Linear transformations

- [[Linear Transformation]]: functions that respect linear combinations, standard matrices,
  composition, and the geometric operators (rotation, reflection, shear, projection)
- [[Kernel and Range]]: what a map destroys and what it can reach, rank, nullity, and
  rank-nullity

### Complex numbers and polar coordinates

- [[Complex Numbers]]: the imaginary unit, arithmetic, conjugates, and why they turn up in a
  linear algebra course at all (a rotation has no real eigenvector)
- [[Polar Form]]: modulus and argument, multiplication as rotate-and-scale, De Moivre's theorem,
  roots of unity, and Euler's formula

## Core Facts to Know

- A linear system has **no solutions, exactly one, or infinitely many**. Never exactly two.
- [[Gaussian Elimination]] is $O(n^3)$ and is how you solve, invert, and find determinants and
  bases. Everything else in the course is either theory or a slower method.
- The three row operations (swap, scale by $c \neq 0$, add a multiple of another row) all
  preserve the solution set. That is why elimination is allowed.
- **Inconsistent** shows up in echelon form as a row reading $0 = c$ for non-zero $c$. **Free
  variables** mean infinitely many solutions, one parameter each.
- [[Matrix Multiplication]] is defined by rows-times-columns because it is **function
  composition**. Inner dimensions must match: $(m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p$.
- $AB \neq BA$. $AB$ is read **right to left**: the rightmost matrix acts first.
- $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$ and $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$. **The order reverses in both.**
- $AB = 0$ does not imply $A = 0$ or $B = 0$, and $AB = AC$ does not imply $B = C$.
- **Vectors are columns** in this vault, with matrices applied on the left: $A\mathbf{x}$. ML
  and statistics code often stores samples as rows and writes $\mathbf{x}A$ instead, which
  transposes every formula.
- $\det A \neq 0$, invertible, columns independent, columns a basis, trivial kernel, rank $n$,
  reduces to $I$, $0$ is not an eigenvalue: **for a square matrix these are all the same
  statement.** See the table in [[Matrix Inverse]].
- $|\det A|$ is the volume scaling factor; the sign records orientation. $\det A = 0$ means the
  transformation collapsed a dimension, which is why it cannot be undone.
- $\det(AB) = \det A \det B$, $\det(A^T) = \det A$, $\det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det A$.
- Cofactor expansion is $O(n!)$, row reduction is $O(n^3)$. Both are correct, only one is usable.
- $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta$. **Zero means orthogonal**,
  which is how perpendicularity extends to $\mathbb{R}^n$ and to functions.
- Every entry of a matrix product is a [[Dot Product]] of a row with a column.
- A **subspace** must contain $\mathbf{0}$ and be closed under both operations. A line missing
  the origin is not one.
- **Independent** and **spanning** are separate conditions. A [[Basis]] is both, and it is the
  exact point where "enough to reach everything" meets "no redundancy".
- Every basis of a space has the same size, and that number is the dimension. More than $n$
  vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are always dependent.
- Coordinates depend on the basis; the vector does not.
- In an **orthonormal** basis, coordinates are found by projecting (one dot product each) instead
  of by solving a system. This is exactly why [[Fourier Series]] works.
- $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$. Eigenvalues come from
  $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$; eigenvectors from solving $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$.
- Eigenvalues sum to the **trace** and multiply to the **determinant**. Free sanity check, use it
  every time.
- Only square matrices have eigenvalues. **Complex eigenvalues mean rotation**, and $\lambda = 0$
  means singular.
- $A$ is diagonalizable when it has $n$ independent eigenvectors. $n$ distinct eigenvalues
  guarantees it; repeated eigenvalues mean check, not fail. Symmetric matrices always are, with
  real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
- $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, which is what makes diagonalization worth the trouble.
- A [[Linear Transformation]] satisfies $T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u})+T(\mathbf{v})$
  and $T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u})$, so **$T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ always**. $f(x) = mx+b$
  with $b \neq 0$ is not linear.
- The **standard matrix** of $T$ has $T(\mathbf{e}_1), \dots, T(\mathbf{e}_n)$ as its columns.
  Hit each basis vector, write down where it lands.
- $\text{rank} + \text{nullity} = $ number of columns. The range is the column space; the kernel
  is the solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$.
- Kernel trivial $\iff$ one-to-one. For a linear map, collapsing anything means collapsing
  something to zero.
- $i^2 = -1$, and in $\mathbb{C}$ every degree-$n$ polynomial has exactly $n$ roots. Complex
  roots of real polynomials come in **conjugate pairs**.
- Divide complex numbers by multiplying through by the conjugate of the denominator.
- In [[Polar Form]] multiplication multiplies moduli and **adds arguments**, so multiplying by
  $z$ is a rotation by $\arg z$ and a scaling by $|z|$. De Moivre and $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta +
  i\sin\theta$ are both that fact restated.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271): [[Sets]] for the set notation underneath [[Vector Space]], and
  [[Proof By Induction]] for the arguments about dimension.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[CALCULUS 2]]: [[Trigonometric Function]] identities are what
  [[Polar Form]] runs on.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101): a [[Group]] and a [[Vector Space]] are the same axiomatic
  move made twice. 2101 also takes [[Complex Numbers]] as a field extension rather than as
  arithmetic.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) is the direct sequel, and it is where most of
  this course is going. The chain runs [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] → [[Spectral Theorem]] →
  [[Singular Value Decomposition]] → [[Principal Component Analysis]], the vault's only route
  from the MATH block into [[MACHINE LEARNING]]. [[Least Squares]] is what replaces
  [[Matrix Inverse|$A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$]] when the system has no solution, [[Projection]] is how it
  is derived, [[Vector Norm]] is where loss functions come from, and [[Pseudoinverse]] answers the
  not-square-or-singular question this course leaves open.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200): [[Vector Calculus]] takes vectors that vary from point to
  point ([[Gradient]], [[Curl]], [[Divergence]]), and [[Differential Equations]] picks up the
  eigenvalue application, where $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ decouples into $n$ scalar equations in
  the eigenvector basis.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199): [[Complex Numbers]] and [[Polar Form]] are the
  prerequisite, and [[Fourier Series]] is an [[Orthogonal Functions|orthonormal basis]] expansion
  in an infinite-dimensional [[Vector Space]] of functions. Its parent already links
  [[Linear Transformation]] for the interval change of variable.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Forward Pass]] is matrix multiplication,
  a neuron is a [[Dot Product]] against its [[Weights]] followed by an
  [[Activation Function]], and [[Back Propagation]] is the chain rule over that structure.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: [[Gaussian Elimination]] at $O(n^3)$ and naive
  [[Matrix Multiplication]] at $O(n^3)$ are the vault's only numerical algorithms to analyse,
  and the $O(n!)$ versus $O(n^3)$ gap for determinants is the cleanest argument for why
  [[Time Complexity]] is worth measuring.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] and [[Leetcode]]: a [[Matrix]] is a 2D [[Array]], and
  [[Matrix Traversal]] reads a grid as a [[Graph]] instead, which is a third reading of the same
  storage.
